TextTranscript: Hello once again friends. It’s good to be with you again for Lesson 5. We’ve simply entitled this lesson The Church. You’ll remember that in our last study we saw how a person responds to God’s love — hearing, believing, repenting, confessing Jesus as Lord, and being baptized into Christ. We also saw that the moment a person is baptized into Christ he is added by the Lord to the number of the saved.

That number is what the New Testament calls the church. So today we’re going to look carefully at what the Bible actually says about the church. Our lesson page organizes everything around eight key headings. You’ll see them listed clearly at the top of the sheet. Let’s walk through them together. Keep your Bibles open and follow along with me.

First, the BUILDER. Matthew 16:18. You’ll find Matthew near the beginning of the New Testament — the first of the four books that tell us about Jesus’ life. Let’s read the verse. “And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.” This comes right after Peter’s confession in verses 13 to 18. Jesus asks the disciples who people say He is. Peter answers, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replies that this truth came from the Father in heaven.

Then He says, “You are Peter” — the Greek word is petros, a stone — “and on this rock” — petra, bedrock — “I will build my church.” You’ll notice on the lower left of the sheet the three key points: Peter’s confession. Jesus identifies it as coming from God. Jesus announces He will build His church upon that rock. Jesus announces He will build His church upon this rock. The New Testament elsewhere tells us that Jesus Christ Himself is the foundation (1 Corinthians 3:11) and the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). The church belongs to Him, and not even the gates of Hades can prevail against it. Jesus is the Builder.

Next, the BEGINNING — Time and Place. Time: “In the last days…” — the Day of Pentecost. Isaiah 2:2-3 prophesied: “In the last days the mountain of the LORD’s temple will be established as the highest of the mountains… The law will go out from Zion, the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.” This was fulfilled on the Day of Pentecost in Acts 2. You’ll find Acts immediately after the four Gospels. The Holy Spirit came with power (Acts 2:1-4), Peter preached the first gospel message, and he quoted Joel:

“In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all people” says (Acts 2:16-17). About three thousand people were baptized and added that day in (Acts 2:41), and the Lord kept adding daily those who were being saved (Acts 2:47). Place: “…out of Zion” — Jerusalem. Exactly as Isaiah foretold, and as Jesus had instructed the apostles to wait in Jerusalem in (Acts 1:4, 8). The church began in Jerusalem on Pentecost, just as prophesied.

Now, OWNER AND HEAD. Owner: Jesus calls it “My church” (Matthew 16:18). Acts 20:28 tells the elders: “Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own blood.” It is Jesus’ body — “the church, which is his body” says (Ephesians 1:22-23; and 1 Corinthians 12:27). Head: Jesus has all authority in (Matthew 28:18). God “appointed him to be head over everything for the church” says (Ephesians 1:22-23). Colossians 1:18 says, “And he is the head of the body, the church… so that in everything he might have the supremacy.” Jesus purchased the church with His blood. He is its owner and its head. He has first place in all things.

DESIGNATIONS — what the Bible calls the church and its members.The Individual:We are called disciples, Christians says (Acts 11:26), saints, and children of God says (Galatians 3:26; and 1 Corinthians 1:2).The Group:The Bible uses many beautiful names:• The church of God / of Christ• The body of Christ says (1 Corinthians 12:27)• The kingdom of Christ• The house of God says (1 Timothy 3:15)No single man-made name captures it all.These designations describe our relationship to Christ and to one another.We are family, a body, a kingdom, and God’s household.

ORGANIZATION. Christ is the head says (Ephesians 1:22-23). Locally, the New Testament shows simple, Spirit-led organization: • Philippians 1:1 — letters addressed “together with the overseers and deacons.” • Acts 14:23 — Paul and Barnabas “appointed elders in every church.” • Acts 20:17, 28 — Paul met with the elders of the Ephesian church and told them the Holy Spirit had made them overseers (shepherds/pastors) to care for the flock. Each congregation is autonomous — self-governing under Christ — with qualified elders (overseers) and deacons serving. There is no earthly headquarters or central hierarchy beyond Christ and His word in the New Testament pattern. The organization is simple, relational, and focused on shepherding God’s people.

WORSHIP. How does the church worship? John 4:24 — “God is spirit, and his worshipers must worship in the Spirit and in truth.” The early church met on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7) to break bread — the Lord’s Supper. Jesus Himself instituted it: “This is my body… This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this in remembrance of me” says  (1 Corinthians 11:23-26). They also sang and prayed with both spirit and understanding in (1 Corinthians 14:15), taught the word, and gave generously. Worship is not about ritual or entertainment. It is heartfelt, Spirit-led, and grounded in truth — centered on remembering Jesus’ death and resurrection. The Lord’s Supper, in particular, keeps the cross at the center every first day of the week.

WORK. What is the church’s work? 1 Timothy 3:15 calls the church “the pillar and foundation of the truth.” We uphold, proclaim, and defend the gospel. James 1:27 adds: “Religion that God our Father accepts as pure and faultless is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.” The church’s work is to stand for truth and to show practical love — caring for the vulnerable while living holy lives. It is both doctrinal and compassionate.

Finally, MEMBERSHIP — how do we become part of the church? On the Day of Pentecost, Peter answered that very question. You’ll recall Acts 2:38: “Repent and be baptized… for the forgiveness of your sins.” Those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added that day (Acts 2:41). Verse 47 tells us the Lord was adding to their number day by day those who were being saved. You’ll notice on the sheet the other references: Acts 20:28 — the church purchased with His blood; Ephesians 5:23 and 25 — Christ is the Savior of the body and gave Himself up for her. When a person is saved, he is added by the Lord to the church. To be in Christ is to be in His body.

We’ve covered a good deal of ground today. The church is not a building or a man-made organization. It is the people Jesus is building, the people He purchased with His own blood, the people He adds to every time someone responds in faith and is baptized. There’s still more we need to see about the church — especially about the individual’s place in it, the special works God has given, and how the early Christians lived and served together. That will be the subject of our next lesson. For now, take the evaluation sheet and follow the usual procedure. Look back over the diagram and the passages we’ve read. When you’re ready, fill in the answers. I commend you for the careful attention you’ve given this study. I look forward to being with you for Lesson 6. Best wishes to you in your continuing study.
